cur:catacombs-priscilla-madonna-prophet.summary: A seated woman holds a child at her breast, while a man beside her raises his hand and points upward, towards a star painted above (outside this crop). The image is usually read as the Virgin nursing the Christ Child with a prophet – Balaam or Isaiah – foretelling his birth, and it is counted among the oldest surviving images of Mary and Jesus.
facts: English Wikipedia notes that the Priscilla catacomb 'may contain the oldest known Marian paintings, from the early third century'.
Commons identifies the pointing man as either Balaam, whose prophecy speaks of a star, or Isaiah, who foretold the birth from a virgin.

Q116272858.summary: The Virgin, veiled and haloed, sits on a cushioned throne between columns, holding the Christ Child upright on her lap; the Child, with his own halo, raises his hand. Two winged angels lean over the canopy above, and a border of acanthus frames the scene. The plaque presents Christ as the incarnate Lord seated in his mother's lap, the throne of the Divine Wisdom.
facts: The Met dates the plaque to 850–875 and attributes it to northern France (accession 17.190.39, gift of J. Pierpont Morgan, 1917).
Its size (14.5 × 8.8 cm) and design match The Met's companion plaque of Christ enthroned with two apostles (17.190.41).
Q116272858.notes: Whether the two Met plaques were originally part of the same object was not verified.

met:473289.summary: Incised into a small cross of green steatite, the crucified Christ stands with arms outstretched and a halo behind his head, his body marked by ribbed lines, while the sun and moon appear above and small winged figures flank his arms. Letters are cut above his head. Simple and worn, this pocket-sized cross carried the image of the Crucifixion into everyday devotion in the Byzantine east.
facts: The Met records it as Byzantine, 11th century, made in Syria, and carved in steatite.
It passed through Ariadne Galleries, New York, to Miriam N. Rosen, who gave it to the Met in 2002.
met:473289.notes: Met 2002.483.4; 8.7 × 5.2 cm. Object type corrected from 'metalwork' to sculpture (stone). The incised letters were not read reliably from the photograph; the flanking figures look like angels but are worn.
